source.text: וְֽ/הָ֨יְתָ֜ה חֶרְפָּ֤ה וּ/גְדוּפָה֙ מוּסָ֣ר וּ/מְשַׁמָּ֔ה לַ/גּוֹיִ֖ם אֲשֶׁ֣ר סְבִיבוֹתָ֑יִ/ךְ בַּ/עֲשׂוֹתִ/י֩ בָ֨/ךְ שְׁפָטִ֜ים בְּ/אַ֤ף וּ/בְ/חֵמָה֙ וּ/בְ/תֹכְח֣וֹת חֵמָ֔ה אֲנִ֥י יְהוָ֖ה דִּבַּֽרְתִּי׃

translation.text: And you shall become[d] a reproach and a taunt, a warning[a] and a horror[b], to the nations that are around you, when I execute judgments on you in anger and in wrath and with wrathful rebukes[c]. I am Yahweh; I have spoken.

footnotes.text: Or 'a warning' could be rendered 'instruction,' 'discipline,' or 'correction'; here it refers to Jerusalem becoming an object lesson to the surrounding nations.
Or 'a horror' may also be understood as 'an object of horror,' 'desolation,' or 'astonishment.'

Hebrew 'she/it shall become'; the translation continues the address to Jerusalem. Greek has 'you shall be.' The Qumran fragment 11Q4 reads והית, whose grammatical interpretation is disputed. The Hebrew source is retained; English 'you' does not establish a second-person Hebrew original.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The retained WLC verb is third feminine singular, plausibly referring to Jerusalem. English continues the direct address with 'you'; this smooths grammatical person rather than reproducing a second-person Hebrew form. Swete's Greek has second singular, while the published 11Q4 spelling והית has competing grammatical interpretations. Note d discloses the difference. Hebrew source priority remains unresolved. The historical HALOT label is retained; no fresh entry consultation is claimed.
'Reproach' preserves both shame and public contempt, fitting prophetic judgment language.
The noun denotes abusive speech or reviling; 'taunt' is concise, readable, and pairs well with 'reproach' without collapsing the distinction.
In this judgment context the sense is not positive instruction alone but an object lesson to others; 'warning' best conveys the exemplary force for the surrounding nations.
The term can denote desolation or appalled astonishment. Here, in a list of what Jerusalem becomes to the nations, 'a horror' captures the reaction provoked by the devastation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to the nations that are around you
lexical_decisions.rationale: This keeps the relational sense of the preposition and the concrete geographic reference to neighboring peoples.

lexical_decisions.chosen: when I execute judgments on you
alternatives: when I carry out judgments against you
when I inflict punishments on you
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive construct with preposition is temporal ('when'). 'Execute judgments' preserves the judicial character of שְׁפָטִים better than the more interpretive 'punishments.'
אַף in divine judgment contexts commonly denotes anger. 'In anger' reads naturally in English while preserving the emotional force.
Using 'wrath' distinguishes חֵמָה from אַף and preserves the intensification of divine judgment.
תוֹכְחוֹת are reproofs/rebukes, and the following חֵמָה qualifies them. 'Wrathful rebukes' is idiomatic and preserves both elements without over-paraphrase.

This entry describes the existing main-text rendering 'I am Yahweh,' consistent with the separate divine-name entry and current project policy. It corrects stale 'the LORD' metadata without changing the main text or newly adjudicating the clause. No fresh HALOT entry consultation is claimed.

Per doctrine, the Tetragrammaton יְהוָה is rendered 'Yahweh' — the transliteration of the divine name — rather than the traditional 'the LORD' substitution. This preserves the personal name God revealed to Israel rather than substituting a title.
The perfect here functions as a solemn divine declaration of certainty. 'I have spoken' is the standard prophetic closure and carries that force well.

theological_decisions.rationale: The verse uses the Tetragrammaton יְהוָה directly. Per updated doctrine, the divine name is rendered 'Yahweh' rather than 'the LORD', preserving the covenant name God revealed at Sinai.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: DOCTRINE.md: Contested terms — יְהוָה YHWH → Yahweh

theological_decisions.issue: Force of מוּסָר in a judgment list
theological_decisions.rationale: The verse presents Jerusalem as an example to surrounding nations after divine judgments. Rendering מוּסָר as 'warning' preserves the exemplary, admonitory force without importing a softer pedagogical sense.

Because the noun appears in a sequence of what Jerusalem becomes 'to the nations,' the emphasis is on the nations' shocked reaction rather than only the city's ruined condition. 'A horror' best preserves that effect in readable English.
